cmc-material.title: Define the drug people will receive
cmc-material.question: Does the evidence describe the preparation people will actually receive?
cmc-material.premise: A drug name does not establish that the material tested before has the same relevant properties as the preparation proposed now.
cmc-material.inherited: You have a candidate and supporting evidence. Their relevance depends on which material was studied.
cmc-material.context: Define the product for this study, including preparation and delivery.

nodes.label: Define the preparation
nodes.question: What is supplied, and what reaches the participant?
nodes.principle: The administered preparation connects chemistry, formulation and delivery.
nodes.body: Describe substance form, composition, strength, route and presentation. Include preparation steps that could change what is delivered. Keep unknown composition explicit.

items.label: Drug substance
items.text: Identity and chemical form

items.label: Drug product
items.text: Composition, strength and presentation

items.label: Administration
items.text: Preparation, route and delivery

nodes.decision: Write one product definition tied to the proposed study.

nodes.label: Locate the differences
nodes.question: How does this preparation differ from the material supporting the evidence?
nodes.principle: Borrowed evidence needs an explicit material comparison.
nodes.body: Compare clinical material with toxicology material, earlier clinical material or a reference product. A shared active ingredient does not answer every formulation or delivery question.

items.label: Evidence material
items.text: What was tested, and under which conditions?

items.label: Proposed material
items.text: What changes in form, vehicle, route or presentation?

items.label: Potential consequence
items.text: Could exposure, local contact or delivered dose change?

nodes.decision: Identify each difference that could alter the meaning of the evidence.

nodes.label: Bridge the consequence
nodes.question: Which comparison would resolve the consequential difference?
nodes.principle: A bridge tests the implication of a change.
nodes.body: Choose evidence suited to the uncertainty: exposure, local compatibility or physical delivery. Comparable systemic exposure answers a narrower question than complete product equivalence.

items.label: Difference
items.text: A material or presentation changes

items.label: Consequence
items.text: A relevant exposure or performance may change

items.label: Bridge evidence
items.text: Measure the consequence the argument depends on

items.label: Supported scope
items.text: State which uncertainty the comparison resolves

nodes.decision: Select evidence that can support or challenge the proposed bridge.

nodes.label: Bound the claim
nodes.question: What may be carried forward, and what remains unresolved?
nodes.principle: An acceptable bridge has a stated scope.
nodes.body: Separate support for this study from support for later formulations, populations or commercial material. Record changes that would reopen the comparison.

items.label: Carry forward
items.text: Evidence applicable to the defined preparation

items.label: Keep open
items.text: Attributes or uses the comparison did not establish

items.label: Revisit after change
items.text: A new form, route, formulation or device may break the bridge

nodes.decision: State the material claim, its limits and the next change that requires reassessment.

cases.name: Ivacaftor
cases.kicker: An exposure comparison with a limited claim
cases.stage: Initial IND 74633 review, reproduced in the 2012 NDA
cases.context: Dog PK compared clinical-associated and nonclinical-associated materials using different stated vehicles. Important material identifiers are redacted.
cases.known: The review reports comparable dog PK for materials in PEG/PVP/KOAc and SLS/methylcellulose/water vehicles.
cases.supports: The comparison supports interpreting systemic exposure across the materials discussed.
cases.uncertain: Redacted identifiers prevent reconstruction of the full formulations. Local tolerability and final commercial-product equivalence are not established here.
cases.decision: Use this as evidence for a specific exposure bridge, with the material and attribute limits visible.
cases.lesson: Different preparations can be connected by relevant evidence without claiming they are identical.

cases.name: Atrovent HFA
cases.kicker: A valve change reopens the comparison
cases.stage: Later IND development after Phase 3; described in the 2004 NDA
cases.context: The proposed inhaler used a third-generation valve after the Phase 3 program had finished.
cases.known: FDA requested further delivery information, particle-size distribution and plume geometry; additional PK and dose-ranging studies were agreed.
cases.supports: The device presentation belonged in the bridge between trial evidence and the proposed product.
cases.uncertain: The public history does not provide full valve specifications. The separate initial IND hold concerned missing Phase 1 data.
cases.decision: Assess the changed delivery attributes and clinical relevance before carrying earlier inhaler evidence forward.
cases.lesson: The active ingredient can stay the same while the evidence needed for the product changes.

exercise.title: A familiar drug, a new presentation
exercise.context: Hypothetical: a team changes the delivery device after completing studies. The active ingredient and nominal strength remain unchanged, but delivered-dose performance has not been compared.
exercise.claim: The earlier evidence fully supports the new presentation because the active ingredient and strength are unchanged.
exercise.prompt: Which response best repairs the argument?

options.label: Carry the evidence forward without further comparison.
options.feedback: The unchanged ingredient and nominal strength do not establish how the new device delivers the preparation.

options.label: Compare delivery attributes, then choose evidence for consequential differences.
options.feedback: This connects the changed presentation to its possible effect and selects a bridge proportionate to the unresolved question.

options.label: Repeat every earlier study before examining the change.
options.feedback: A complete repetition is not justified merely by a change. First establish which attributes and conclusions may be affected.

result.claim: Earlier evidence may support the new presentation if consequential delivery differences are adequately bridged.
result.support: The ingredient and nominal strength match; the delivery comparison is still needed.
result.uncertainty: The new device may alter the delivered preparation or dose.
result.next: Compare performance and choose additional evidence for any consequential difference.

boundary.required: IND CMC information must support identity, strength, quality and purity at the proposed stage.
boundary.recommended: FDA recommends explaining differences between clinical and toxicology products and their possible safety implications.
boundary.judgment: Choose the comparison that resolves the relevant consequence; a formulation difference does not automatically require repeating every study.

recommendationSource.label: FDA Phase 1 IND guidance · PDF 6–7; cites 21 CFR 312.23(a)(7)

handoff.label: Make this material consistently
handoff.text: Carry the product definition and material bridge into tests, limits and controls that support consistent clinical supply.

cmc-controls.title: Make and control consistent material
cmc-controls.question: Can the process and controls reliably produce material whose relevant properties are understood?
cmc-controls.premise: A test result supports release only when the method, acceptance rule and manufacturing knowledge address the properties that matter for use.
cmc-controls.inherited: The clinical preparation is defined, and differences from supporting materials have a stated bridge.
cmc-controls.context: Turn product and process knowledge into a defensible decision about each clinical batch.

nodes.label: Trace possible variation
nodes.question: What could change between batches, and why would it matter?
nodes.principle: Controls begin with a plausible source of consequential variation.
nodes.body: Consider materials, process steps and resulting attributes. Connect impurities or performance changes to exposure and use. Distinguish an identified hazard from an unresolved signal.

items.label: Source of variation
items.text: Material, process step or equipment

items.label: Product attribute
items.text: Impurity, strength or release performance

items.label: Consequence
items.text: Potential effect on clinical exposure or safety

nodes.decision: Name the variation to prevent, detect or qualify.

nodes.label: Give tests jobs
nodes.question: What decision is each test intended to support?
nodes.principle: A useful method must distinguish what the decision depends on.
nodes.body: Separate development experiments, patient-acceptability assessments and routine release tests. Show that the chosen method can detect a meaningful difference before interpreting a passing result.

items.label: Development
items.text: Understand how formulation or process affects performance

items.label: Release
items.text: Decide whether this batch meets justified criteria

items.label: Patient experience
items.text: Assess an acceptability claim with relevant evidence

nodes.decision: Keep tests with a defined purpose and evidence that they can perform it.

nodes.label: Justify the limit
nodes.question: Why is the proposed acceptance rule appropriate for this use?
nodes.principle: Limits connect measured attributes with a safety or performance basis.
nodes.body: Distinguish observed batch values from permitted limits. Consider dose, route and duration when interpreting impurity exposure. A favorable result cannot repair a method that misses the relevant change.

items.label: Measured attribute
items.text: A result from a suitable method

items.label: Use conditions
items.text: Dose, route and duration

items.label: Acceptance basis
items.text: Evidence supporting the permitted range

nodes.decision: Explain what supports the limit and what further evidence or tighter control is needed.

nodes.label: Respond to change
nodes.question: What happens when results or manufacturing changes challenge the control strategy?
nodes.principle: A control strategy includes investigation and reassessment.
nodes.body: Investigate failures and unexpected trends. Compare changed material with the evidence supporting use. Revise the method, process, limit or qualification argument when its basis no longer holds.

items.label: Signal
items.text: Failure, trend or planned manufacturing change

items.label: Investigation
items.text: Distinguish plausible causes with evidence

items.label: Response
items.text: Correct the cause and reassess affected claims

items.label: Continuity
items.text: Document which evidence still applies

nodes.decision: Define the action that follows a failed rule or a consequential change.

cases.name: Vamorolone
cases.kicker: An impurity signal changes initial permission
cases.stage: Initial IND 118942, 2014–2015; described in the 2023 NDA
cases.context: The initial submission contained two drug-substance impurities with structural alerts for genotoxicity.
cases.known: FDA placed the IND on partial clinical hold in January 2015. Completed genotoxicity studies were submitted, and the hold was removed in March.
cases.supports: Uncertainty about impurities can materially affect whether proposed clinical work may proceed.
cases.uncertain: This history does not disclose impurity identities or test results. Hold removal does not establish that every alert was a false positive.
cases.decision: Address the impurity uncertainty with relevant evidence; preserve the distinction between a structural alert and an established hazard.
cases.lesson: The active substance’s evidence does not automatically cover everything present in the batch.

cases.name: ACER-001
cases.kicker: A test needs the right job
cases.context: The sponsor proposed taste-mask coating testing alongside dissolution controls for sodium phenylbutyrate.
cases.known: FDA requested discriminating dissolution methods and multi-timepoint data. It clarified that exploratory taste-coating integrity testing was not required routine QC.
cases.supports: Development understanding, taste acceptability and batch release were separate questions requiring appropriate evidence.
cases.uncertain: Final specifications remained an NDA review issue. Coating details are partly redacted.
cases.decision: Establish adequate coating controls and a discriminating dissolution method; use patient-relevant evidence for taste-specific acceptability claims.
cases.lesson: More tests do not improve control unless they answer a useful question.

exercise.title: A passing result that cannot discriminate
exercise.context: Hypothetical: a candidate dissolution method gives the same result for batches independently shown to release drug differently. The team proposes the method for batch release.
exercise.claim: All batches pass, so the method establishes consistent release performance.
exercise.prompt: What is the strongest next decision?

options.label: Accept the method because every tested batch passes.
options.feedback: A passing result is uninformative when the method cannot reveal a difference relevant to the intended release decision.

options.label: Tighten the numerical limit without changing the method.
options.feedback: A narrower rule does not make an insensitive measurement distinguish relevant differences.

options.label: Establish a method that detects relevant release differences, then justify its acceptance rule.
options.feedback: Method capability comes before interpreting compliance. Development comparisons should show that the test can support the proposed batch decision.

result.claim: The current method does not establish consistent release performance.
result.support: Independent evidence shows differences that the candidate method does not detect.
result.uncertainty: A suitable method and justified acceptance rule remain to be established.
result.next: Evaluate discriminating methods using relevant batch differences, then define the release criterion.

boundary.required: Most Phase 1 investigational drugs remain subject to statutory CGMP despite their Part 211 exemption; scope exclusions apply.
boundary.recommended: FDA recommends appropriate QC responsibilities and reliable laboratory testing for Phase 1 material.
boundary.judgment: Choose controls proportionate to the product and study; neither an uncontrolled process nor a universal commercial validation package follows from phase-appropriate quality.

handoff.label: Preserve suitable material
handoff.text: Carry the justified attributes and limits into storage, preparation and delivery, where time and handling may change the product.

cmc-stability.title: Keep the product suitable through dosing
cmc-stability.question: Does the quality evidence cover the product’s entire journey to administration?
cmc-stability.premise: Suitability at release does not establish suitability after storage, preparation or delivery. Each transition can change the material or the evidence that applies.
cmc-stability.inherited: The product has a defined identity and justified controls for clinical supply.
cmc-stability.context: Follow the preparation from manufacture through the last administration supported by the evidence.

nodes.label: Map the journey
nodes.question: Which conditions and times must the evidence cover?
nodes.principle: A stability claim names its material, conditions and duration.
nodes.body: Trace storage, shipping, preparation, waiting and delivery. Distinguish unopened shelf life from the period after dilution or transfer. Use the actual proposed clinical procedure.

items.label: Supply
items.text: Container, storage and shipment

items.label: Preparation
items.text: Thaw, dilute or transfer as applicable

items.label: In use
items.text: Waiting conditions and duration

items.label: Administration
items.text: Material delivered through the intended system

nodes.decision: Specify the supported conditions and duration for each segment.

nodes.label: Look beyond assay
nodes.question: What could make the product unsuitable even if its active content remains acceptable?
nodes.principle: Stability includes chemical, physical, microbial and delivery performance.
nodes.body: Select relevant failure modes for this product. A container may contribute particles; dilution may cause aggregation; a device may alter delivery. Test the property whose change would matter.

items.label: Chemical
items.text: Active loss or increasing degradants

items.label: Physical
items.text: Particles, precipitation or aggregation

items.label: Microbial
items.text: Protection through the proposed storage and use

items.label: Delivery
items.text: Dose or performance after handling

nodes.decision: Match each plausible failure to evidence collected under relevant conditions.

nodes.label: Set usable boundaries
nodes.question: What instructions follow, and what would invalidate them?
nodes.principle: Instructions should preserve the conditions demonstrated by evidence.
nodes.body: Translate findings into storage, preparation, in-use duration and delivery instructions. A new diluent, container or procedure can reopen the claim. Preserve uncertainty about causes that remain unresolved.

items.label: Evidence
items.text: Performance under tested conditions

items.label: Instruction
items.text: Use conditions the evidence supports

items.label: Change trigger
items.text: A different container, diluent or delivery procedure

nodes.decision: State the supported procedure and when reassessment is required.

cases.name: Lenacapavir
cases.stage: Later IND full holds in December 2021; subsequent NDA resubmission review
cases.context: Borosilicate vials showed incompatibility with lenacapavir injection, surface degradation and glass particles.
cases.known: FDA lacked information to assess injection risk and possible particulate contribution to persistent local reactions. Later review addressed alternative packaging, light protection and in-use stability.
cases.supports: Container compatibility and preparation conditions belonged in the safety and stability assessment.
cases.uncertain: Glass particles were a possible contributor to local reactions, not an established cause of every reaction.
cases.decision: Investigate the particle exposure and support the proposed presentation through expiry and preparation; do not assume a container substitution alone resolves every concern.
cases.lesson: The package can change what is administered, even when the active ingredient is unchanged.

sources.label: Resubmission storage and in-use assessment · PDF 83

cases.name: Cytalux
cases.stage: 2021 NDA quality review describing IND experience; initial IND timing not established
cases.context: Pafolacianine prepared with saline was associated with hypersensitivity reactions in IND participants.
cases.known: The investigation identified aggregation as the most likely explanation. The reviewed instructions specified 5% dextrose only, with supported storage and preparation conditions.
cases.supports: Diluent compatibility can determine whether an administration procedure is supported.
cases.uncertain: The causal explanation remains qualified. The NDA review does not disclose the original IND stability package.
cases.decision: Use the supported diluent and preparation conditions. Treat a proposed substitution as a new compatibility question.
cases.lesson: A preparation instruction is part of the quality argument, not an incidental detail.

exercise.title: A convenient diluent substitution
exercise.context: Hypothetical: stability evidence supports a product in its vial and after dilution with one specified diluent. A clinical site proposes another diluent. Compatibility after substitution has not been evaluated.
exercise.claim: The substitute is acceptable because the undiluted vial remains stable.
exercise.prompt: Which decision follows from the available evidence?

options.label: Use the substitute because the vial passed stability testing.
options.feedback: Vial stability does not establish compatibility after a different dilution step. The material and conditions have changed.

options.label: Keep the supported preparation while evaluating compatibility of the proposed substitute.
options.feedback: This preserves the demonstrated procedure and identifies the evidence needed before extending the claim to different preparation conditions.

options.label: Extend unopened-vial storage testing to establish the substitute’s compatibility.
options.feedback: More time in the original container does not test the transformation introduced by the new diluent.

result.claim: The existing evidence supports the specified preparation, not the proposed diluent substitution.
result.support: The tested vial and specified diluted preparation remained suitable under their assessed conditions.
result.uncertainty: The substitute may change physical, chemical or other relevant properties.
result.next: Evaluate the alternative preparation before revising administration instructions.

boundary.required: IND stability information must support the planned studies; the needed extent depends on the product and investigation.
boundary.recommended: FDA recommends representative Phase 1 stability work covering manufacture through last administration and protective storage, handling and shipping.
boundary.judgment: Choose relevant conditions and failure modes. A commercial registration stability package is not a universal initial IND requirement.

recommendationSource.label: FDA Phase 1 CGMP guidance · PDF 13–14; cites 21 CFR 312.23(a)(7)

handoff.label: Make dosing operational
handoff.text: Carry the supported strength, preparation, delivery conditions and use period into the clinical dosing plan.
